name: Inside Heel Hook
description: Master Inside Heel Hook from 50-50 Guard. Rotational knee attack using inside leg control. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Inside Heel Hook is a devastating rotational knee attack executed from 50-50 Guard and other leg entanglement positions. This submission targets the knee joint through rotational force applied to the heel, making it one of the most effective and dangerous techniques in modern grappling. The attack derives its name from the direction of rotation—an inside heel hook rotates the heel toward the opponent's centerline, attacking the lateral structures of the knee including the ACL, MCL, and meniscus.

From 50-50 Guard Top, the inside heel hook becomes available when you establish inside position control and secure grip access to your opponent's heel. The key mechanical principle involves creating a figure-four configuration with your arms around the opponent's heel while their leg is trapped by your leg entanglement. The finish requires coordinated hip extension, shoulder rotation, and arm squeeze to generate rotational force through the opponent's knee.

This submission has revolutionized modern leg lock systems and is a cornerstone of contemporary no-gi grappling strategy. Its effectiveness stems from the difficulty of defending once proper control is established—the rotational force can cause immediate joint damage before the defender can react. This potency makes the inside heel hook both highly effective and requiring exceptional responsibility regarding partner safety and tap recognition.
key_principles: Inside position must be established before attempting heel exposure—your leg controls determine your ability to attack
Heel cup grip is non-negotiable: fingers wrap around the heel while wrist locks against the Achilles tendon
Hip extension drives the primary rotational force, not arm strength alone
Keep your elbows tight to your body throughout the finish to maximize torque transmission
The heel must be pulled toward your chest while simultaneously rotating toward opponent's centerline
Control the knee line—opponent's knee should be trapped below your armpit to prevent rotation escape
Recognize the difference between heel slip (reattack) and defensive rotation (transition or release)
setup_requirements: 50-50 Guard Top position established with inside leg control secured
Two-handed grip access to opponent's heel with their foot exposed past your shoulder line
Opponent's knee trapped below your armpit or controlled by your leg triangle
Your hips positioned to allow full extension during the finish
Inside position confirmed—your knee angle prevents opponent from matching inside control

execution_steps.description: Confirm your inside leg maintains the dominant angle against opponent's leg structure. Your shin or calf should create inside pressure that prevents them from gaining inside control. This is the fundamental requirement before any heel hook attempt.

Reach across opponent's leg with your primary hand, cupping their heel with fingers wrapped around the heel bone. Your wrist should lock against their Achilles tendon, creating a secure anchor point that prevents heel extraction.

Bring your secondary hand to grip your own wrist or forearm, creating a figure-four configuration around the heel. Your elbows should squeeze together, keeping the grip structure tight against your chest with no space for heel escape.

Pull opponent's leg tight to your body so their knee sits below your armpit. Clamp down with your elbow and upper arm to prevent their knee from rotating to relieve pressure. This knee control is essential for the finish.

Initiate hip extension while simultaneously rotating your shoulders toward opponent's opposite hip. The heel should travel in an arc toward your shoulder as you extend. Keep elbows squeezed tight to transmit force efficiently.

Continue hip extension and shoulder rotation until opponent taps or you feel the submission is secure. Your hips drive forward, chest stays up, and the heel rotates toward opponent's centerline. Release immediately upon tap—there is minimal warning before joint damage.

common_counters.counter: Hide heel by rotating knee inward and tucking foot close to body
common_counters.your_response: If heel disappears within 3-5 seconds, immediately transition to kneebar, back take, or different leg entanglement rather than chasing the hidden heel

common_counters.counter: Strip grips before figure-four is established using two-on-one grip fighting
common_counters.your_response: Accelerate grip sequence and immediately establish figure-four. Once figure-four is locked, grip strips become much more difficult. Maintain constant pressure to prevent defensive grip establishment

common_counters.counter: Roll with the rotation to relieve pressure and escape the entanglement
common_counters.your_response: Follow their roll by maintaining hip pressure and leg control. Their rolling motion often exposes the heel further or creates back take opportunity. Do not release grips during their roll

common_counters.counter: Match inside position to neutralize attacking angle
common_counters.your_response: If opponent successfully matches inside position, the heel hook attack becomes unavailable. Immediately transition to Outside Ashi-Garami or disengage to reset leg entanglement with superior inside control

common_errors.error: Attempting heel hook without established inside position control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily defends by matching inside position or counters with their own heel hook attack
common_errors.correction: Always confirm inside position before initiating grip sequence. If inside position is contested, address that first through leg fighting before pursuing the submission

common_errors.error: Using arm strength alone without hip extension for the finish
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient rotational force to finish against resisting opponent, leads to grip fatigue and failed submission
common_errors.correction: Drive finish through hip extension and shoulder rotation. Your legs and hips generate far more power than your arms. Keep elbows tight and let hip drive create the rotation

common_errors.error: Allowing space between elbows during the figure-four grip
common_errors.consequence: Heel slips free from loose grip structure, opponent escapes or you lose control
common_errors.correction: Squeeze elbows together throughout the entire sequence. The figure-four should feel like a vice with no space for heel movement. Pull heel tight to your chest

common_errors.error: Continuing to chase heel hook when opponent successfully hides their heel
common_errors.consequence: Wasting energy and positional advantage while opponent recovers or counters
common_errors.correction: Set a 3-5 second rule—if heel exposure fails within this window, immediately transition to alternative attacks like kneebar, back take, or different leg entanglement

common_errors.error: Failing to control the knee line allowing opponent's knee to rotate freely
common_errors.consequence: Opponent relieves rotational pressure by spinning their knee, negating the submission
common_errors.correction: Trap opponent's knee below your armpit and clamp with your elbow. Their knee must remain relatively fixed for rotational force to affect the joint

training_progressions.description: Practice heel cup grip and figure-four configuration on a compliant partner. Focus on proper hand placement, elbow squeeze, and pulling heel tight to chest. No finishing pressure—just grip establishment and release.

Add hip extension and shoulder rotation to the finish with partner who taps immediately upon any pressure. Develop coordination between grip squeeze, hip drive, and rotation. Partner provides light positional resistance but taps at first hint of pressure.

Practice entering heel hook from various 50-50 scrambles. Partner defends with heel hiding and grip fighting. Work counter-sequences: heel hook to kneebar, heel hook to back take. Medium resistance on entries, immediate tap on submissions.

Apply heel hook in positional sparring starting from 50-50. Both partners must have mature understanding of tap timing and injury risk. Focus on entry timing, recognizing when to attack versus transition, and developing submission chain mentality.

variants_and_adaptations.description: After establishing heel control, rotate belly-down while maintaining figure-four grip. This variation increases control and finishing power by using full body rotation rather than just hip extension. Particularly effective when opponent attempts to roll with standard heel hook.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent defends by rolling or when additional control is needed against larger opponents

variants_and_adaptations.description: Use a palm-to-palm grip rather than figure-four, with hands clasped around the heel. Faster to establish but offers less control. Often used as initial attack to force reaction before transitioning to stronger grip configuration.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Quick attack opportunity when opponent's heel is briefly exposed, or to set up transitions

variants_and_adaptations.description: Apply inside heel hook from Inside Ashi-Garami position rather than 50-50. The mechanics remain identical but the leg entanglement offers different control characteristics and entry options.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When Inside Ashi-Garami is achieved through sweep or entry rather than 50-50

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of the Inside Heel Hook?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to apply rotational force to the opponent's knee joint by rotating their heel toward their centerline. This attacks the lateral knee structures including ACL, MCL, and meniscus, forcing a tap or causing joint damage if the opponent fails to submit.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must inside position be established before attempting the heel hook?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Inside position control determines your ability to attack and prevents opponent counter-attacks. Without inside position, your opponent can match your leg angle to neutralize your attack or launch their own heel hook. Inside control is the gatekeeper that enables all offensive heel hook opportunities.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips needed for Inside Heel Hook?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary grip is a heel cup where fingers wrap around the heel bone with wrist locked against the Achilles tendon. The secondary hand creates a figure-four by gripping your own wrist or forearm. Elbows squeeze together, pulling the heel configuration tight to your chest with no space for escape.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent successfully hides their heel by tucking it close to their body—what should you do?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Apply the 3-5 second rule: if heel exposure fails within this window, immediately transition to alternative attacks. Options include kneebar by controlling above the knee, back take by releasing legs and circling, or transition to different leg entanglement like Inside Ashi-Garami for better angles. Do not stubbornly chase a well-defended heel.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you generate finishing power for the heel hook—arms or hips?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Hip extension generates the primary finishing power, not arm strength. Your arms maintain grip structure and transmit force, but the rotation comes from driving your hips forward while rotating your shoulders. This generates far more torque than arms alone and prevents grip fatigue during extended sequences.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the function of controlling the knee line during the finish?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Controlling the knee line by trapping opponent's knee below your armpit prevents them from spinning their knee to relieve rotational pressure. If their knee can rotate freely, the torque dissipates through leg movement rather than affecting the joint. The knee must remain relatively fixed for the submission to work.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent begins rolling with your heel hook rotation—how do you respond?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Follow their roll by maintaining hip pressure and grip control. Do not release your grips during their roll. Their rolling motion often exposes the heel further as they rotate or creates an opportunity to take their back as they turn away. Stay connected and look for the improved angle or transition.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Inside Heel Hook from 50-50?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is immediately after confirming inside position when opponent's heel is exposed past your shoulder line. Attack during opponent's transitions when their focus shifts—such as when they attempt to establish their own grips or try to escape the entanglement. Avoid attacking when opponent has strong heel defense established.

knowledge_assessment.question: What differentiates the belly-down finish from the standard heel hook finish?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The belly-down finish involves rotating your entire body face-down while maintaining the figure-four grip. This increases control by pinning opponent's leg with your body weight and generates more rotational force through full torso rotation. It's particularly effective against opponents who try to roll with standard heel hooks or when facing larger, stronger defenders.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you safely train Inside Heel Hook with a partner?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Begin with grip mechanics only and no finishing pressure. Progress to light resistance where partner taps at first hint of pressure. Both partners must understand that heel hooks offer minimal warning before joint damage—tap early and release immediately. Only apply full resistance heel hooks with experienced partners who have mature tap timing. Never ego-test heel hooks.

safety_considerations: The Inside Heel Hook is one of the most dangerous submissions in grappling due to the rapid onset of joint damage with minimal warning. The rotational force attacks ligaments (ACL, MCL) and meniscus that provide minimal pain feedback before injury occurs. Partners must tap early—waiting until it hurts often means damage has already occurred. Release immediately upon tap with no additional pressure. Never ego-test heel hooks or refuse to tap. Training should progress from zero resistance through graduated stages. Both partners should verbally confirm understanding of tap timing before positional sparring. The attacker bears responsibility for controlled application. Avoid heel hooks when fatigued, as reaction times suffer. Consider the legal status in your competition ruleset—IBJJF restricts heel hooks by belt level. Any knee pain or instability after training requires immediate medical evaluation.
position_integration: The Inside Heel Hook represents the primary finishing threat within the 50-50 Guard system and modern leg lock methodology. From 50-50 Top, the heel hook creates constant submission pressure that forces defensive reactions, opening transition opportunities. When the heel hook is defended through heel hiding, kneebar and back take become available. When opponent tries to match inside position, Outside Ashi-Garami transitions provide new angles. The technique chains seamlessly with other leg entanglements—Inside Ashi-Garami, Saddle, and Outside Ashi-Garami all offer heel hook opportunities with different control characteristics. Understanding this submission is essential for both offense and defense in any leg lock engagement, as it remains the highest-percentage finish once proper control is established.
